questions.q: What does the transformation layer actually do, in this lesson's terms?
options: Turns raw, ingested (bronze) data into clean, conformed (silver) and business-ready aggregated (gold) data
Handles getting data from a source into storage for the first time
Serves final query results directly to dashboards
Decides whether ingestion should be batch or streaming
questions.explain: This is Databricks & Delta Lake Lesson 25's bronze -> silver -> gold shape, applied as a system design component.

questions.q: Why must a bronze-to-silver transformation step be idempotent?
options: A rerun on the same batch (a retry or manual fix-and-rerun) must not duplicate rows, which plain append would allow to happen silently
Idempotency only matters for the ingestion layer, not transformation
Silver tables cannot use MERGE under any circumstances
Idempotency is optional for transformation as long as gold is correct
questions.explain: This is Lesson 11's principle applied specifically here, using Databricks Lesson 29's exact MERGE-on-natural-key mechanism.

questions.q: According to Databricks Lesson 30, why might a gold table use overwrite instead of MERGE?
options: For a small table that's cheap to rebuild from all of silver each run, overwrite is simpler and just as correct as MERGE
Overwrite is always required for every gold table, regardless of size
MERGE cannot technically be used on gold tables
Overwrite guarantees better idempotency than MERGE ever could
questions.explain: A genuinely large gold aggregate still needs the same incremental MERGE approach silver uses — the choice depends on rebuild cost.

questions.q: What are the two concrete mechanisms Databricks Lesson 31 covers for knowing what data is actually new?
options: A manually maintained watermark column, or Delta's own Change Data Feed reading the transaction log
A random sampling of rows and a manual spot-check
Re-scanning the entire bronze table on every single run
Asking the source system to flag new rows itself, with no other mechanism
questions.explain: Choosing 'incremental' only answers half the design question — a concrete mechanism for detecting new data still has to be designed in.

questions.q: Why does silver almost always need incremental processing, unlike some gold tables?
options: New bronze rows keep arriving continuously, so fully rewriting silver every run would waste significant work
Silver tables are always too small to justify incremental processing
Silver and gold always use the identical refresh strategy
Incremental processing is impossible for silver tables specifically
questions.explain: Unlike a small gold aggregate that's cheap to fully rebuild, silver is fed continuously by bronze, making a full rewrite each run wasteful.
